DECISION AND OPINION ON REVIEW 
Timely Petition for Review under §19(b) having been filed by the Petitioner and 
Respondent herein and notice given to all parties, the Commission, after considering the issues of 
accident, causal connection, medical expenses, penalties and fees, temporary total disability, and 
being advised of the facts and law, affirms and adopts the Decision of the Arbitrator, which is 
attached hereto and made a part hereof.  The Commission further remands this case to the 
Arbitrator for further proceedings for a determination of a further amount of temporary total 
compensation or of compensation for permanent disability, if any, pursuant to Thomas v. Industrial 
Commission, 78 Ill.2d 327, 399 N.E.2d 1322, 35 Ill.Dec. 794 (1980). 
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Decision of the 
Arbitrator filed October 14, 2025, is hereby affirmed and adopted. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that this case be remanded to the 
Arbitrator for further proceedings consistent with this Decision, but only after the latter of 
expiration of the time for filing a written request for Summons to the Circuit Court has expired 
without the filing of such a written request, or after the time of completion of any judicial 
proceedings, if such a written request has been filed.

DISSENT 
Petitioner’s claim for workers’ compensation benefits should be barred under Section 11 
of the Act, which states: 
Accidental injuries incurred while participating in voluntary 
recreational programs including but not limited to athletic events, 
parties and picnics do not arise out of and in the course of the 
employment even though the employer pays some or all of the cost 
thereof. This exclusion shall not apply in the event that the injured 
employee was ordered or assigned by his employer to participate in 
the program. 820 ILCS 305/11. 
There is no dispute that the CTA Jamboree held on September 7, 2024 was a recreational 
event. The primary issue in this claim was whether Petitioner’s participation was voluntary or 
whether she was ordered or assigned to participate. (Petitioner’s Brief, pg. 10; Respondent’s Brief, 
pg. 11). 
An employer’s control over the recreational activity may corroborate a claim that an 
employee’s participation was ordered or assigned, but it is not, of itself, sufficient to either

demonstrate that fact or support an award of benefits independent of proof of an employer’s 
assignment or direction to participate in the activity. Pickett v. Indus. Comm’n, 252 Ill. App. 3d 
355, 359 (1993); see also Gooden v. Indus. Comm’n, 366 Ill. App. 3d 1064, 1066 (2006). Similarly, 
evidence of an employer’s support for and the benefit derived from recreational activities it 
sponsors is insufficient to render an injury compensable. The statute explicitly excludes coverage 
even if some or all of the costs of the recreational activity are borne by the employer. Pickett v. 
Indus. Comm’n, 252 Ill. App. 3d 355, 357-58 (1993). Therefore, the fact that Respondent organized 
the event, held it on CTA grounds, paid certain vendors, and paid for the awards, banquet and 
food, is not dispositive of the issue. Under Section 11, Petitioner’s injuries are not compensable 
unless she was ordered or assigned by Respondent to participate as a judge at the CTA Jamboree. 
 
Petitioner argues that her attendance was not voluntary because Chris Otero, a senior 
manager in a different department and not her direct supervisor, ordered and assigned her to attend 
the event. She also claimed that she had to arrive at the event at 6:00 a.m. (before it opened to the 
public) and wear her personal protective equipment (PPE) unlike other attendees. According to the 
record, Petitioner testified that Mr. Otero called her on her day off and asked her to judge a 
competition at the event. Her testimony further indicated that Mr. Otero only called her once about 
4-5 months prior to the event. At arbitration, Petitioner was asked several times whether she was 
a volunteer, and she provided the same answer: that she was asked to be a judge and she 
participated as a judge. She denied being forced to attend the event. 
 
By these facts, Petitioner was asked (once) to participate in the CTA Jamboree with no 
repercussion for declining. She was given a choice, not an order or assignment. Likewise, the 
instructions to show up at 6:00 a.m. and wear her PPE gear were simply what was required in her 
capacity as a judge for the signal department competition. These instructions were not an order or 
assignment by Respondent to attend the event and judge a competition. 
 
Respondent’s witnesses, Jeannine Messina and Elric Erving, corroborated the voluntary 
nature of Petitioner’s participation in the event. They testified that volunteers could either fill out 
an online application or discuss with their management team about volunteering. They also 
confirmed that there were no repercussions for an employee to decline to attend and volunteers 
were not paid. Mr. Erving stated that there was no pressure to participate and employees were able 
to decline or accept. Ms. Messina further confirmed that depending on the competition, an 
employee could be required to wear safety gear while volunteering. 
 
Based on the preponderance of the evidence, I find that Petitioner’s participation in the 
CTA Jamboree on September 7, 2024 was completely voluntary, and pursuant to Section 11, her 
injury on that date did not arise out of and in the course of the employment. For these reasons, I 
dissent. 
 
 
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
/s/ Christopher A. Harris

An Application for Adjustment of Claim was filed in this matter, and a Notice of Hearing was 
electronically mailed to each party.  The matter was heard by the Honorable Joseph D. Amarilio, 
Arbitrator of the Commission, in the city of Chicago, Illinois on July 29, 2025.  After reviewing 
all of the evidence presented, the Arbitrator hereby makes findings on the disputed issues checked 
below and attaches those findings to this document. 
 
DISPUTED ISSUES 
 
C. Did an accident occur that arose out of and in the course of Petitioner's employment by 
Respondent? 
 
 
 
F. Is Petitioner's current condition of ill-being causally related to the injury? 
 
 
J. Were the medical services that were provided to Petitioner reasonable and necessary? Has 
Respondent paid all appropriate charges for all reasonable and necessary medical services? 
 
 
L.  What temporary benefits are in dispute? 
 
        TPD  
       Maintenance 
X TTD 
 
M. Should penalties or fees be imposed upon Respondent?  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
FINDINGS 
 
On the date of accident, 9/7/2024, Respondent was operating under and subject to the provisions 
of the Act.   
 
On this date, an employee-employer relationship did exist between Petitioner and Respondent.   
 
On this date, Petitioner did sustain an accident that arose out of and in the course of employment. 
 
Timely notice of this accident was given to Respondent. 
 
Petitioner's current condition of ill-being is causally related to the accident. 
 
26IWCC0130

Page 2 of 16 
 
In the year preceding the injury, Petitioner earned $128,141.00; the average weekly wage was 
$2,464.25. 
 
On the date of accident, Petitioner was 44 years of age, single with 0 dependent children. 
 
Respondent has not paid all reasonable and necessary charges for all reasonable and necessary 
medical services.   
 
Respondent has paid $5,474.00 in non-occupational indemnity disability benefits and $2,047.14 
in other benefits, for which credit may be allowed under Section 8(j) of the Act.  
 
ORDER 
 
Respondent shall pay Petitioner temporary total disability benefits of $1,642.83 per week for 43-
1/7th  weeks, commencing September 8, 2024 through July 6, 2025 , as provided in Section 8(b) 
of the Act.    Respondent shall make this payment directly to Petitioner’s attorney in accordance 
with Section 9080.20 of the Rules Governing Practice before the Illinois Workers’ Compensation 
Commission. 
 
Respondent shall pay reasonable and necessary medical services, pursuant to the medical fee 
schedule, of $73,993.32 to Northwestern Medicine, $17,093.00 to Athletico Physical Therapy,  as 
provided in Sections 8(a) and 8.2 of the Act.  Respondent shall make this payment directly to 
Petitioner’s attorney in accordance with Section 9080.20 of the Rules Governing Practice before 
the Illinois Workers’ Compensation Commission. 
 
Petitioner  is not entitled to penalties under the Act. Therefore, Respondent is not liable  pay to 
Petitioner attorney  fees under Section 16 of the Act nor penalties under Section 19(k)  nor Section 
19(l) of the Act.   
 
In no instance shall this award be a bar to subsequent hearing and determination of an additional 
amount of temporary total disability, maintenance benefits, medical benefits, or compensation for 
a permanent disability, if any.   
 
RULES REGARDING APPEALS  Unless a party files a Petition for Review within 30 days after 
receipt of this decision, and perfects a review in accordance with the Act and Rules, then this 
decision shall be entered as the decision of the Commission.   
 
STATEMENT OF INTEREST RATE  If the Commission reviews this award, interest at the rate set 
forth on the Notice of Decision of Arbitrator shall accrue from the date listed below to the day 
before the date of payment; however, if an employee's appeal results in either no change or a 
decrease in this award, interest shall not accrue.

ATTACHMENT TO ARBITRATION DECISION  
LAHORI v. CTA    24 WC 025546 
 
FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW 
 
I. 
 PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
Ms. Schieta Lahori  (Petitioner), by and through her attorneys, filed an Application for Adjustment 
of Claim for benefits under the Illinois Workers' Compensation Act (“Act” ) (820 ILCS 305/1 et 
seq.). Petitioner alleged that she sustained accidental injuries that arose out of and in the course of 
her employment with the Chicago Transit Authority  (Respondent). 
 
The hearing proceeded pursuant to Section 19 (b) of the Act on July 29, 2025 on the following  
disputed issues: (1) Whether Petitioner sustained an accident  that arose out of and in the course 
of  her  employment. (2) Whether Petitioner’s current condition of ill-being is causally related to 
the injury.  (3) Whether the medical services provided to Petitioner were reasonable and necessary.  
(4) Whether Petitioner is entitled to temporary total disability benefits. (5) Whether Respondent is 
liable for fees and penalties under Section 16, 19(k) and 19(l) of the Act.  The parties mutually 
requested a written decision, including findings of fact and conclusions of law (Arb. Ex. 1). 
 
The threshold issue in this case is whether Petitioner, a CTA electrical lineman who was injured 
while serving as a judge at Respondent's annual jamboree/rodeo, sustained an injury that arose out 
of and within the scope of her employment when the accident occurred. The key factual  dispute 
concerns whether Petitioner's participation in the event was a voluntary, as Respondent contends, 
or whether she was directed or required by her employer to participate in the program. 
 
II. 
FINDINGS OF FACT  
 
A. Testimony of Petitioner  
Petitioner has been employed by Respondent for almost five years as an electrical lineman and has 
been based  out of the west shop (T. p. 11). Her position involves working on electrical equipment, 
including the third rail; working at train stations, platforms, and mezzanines, performing 
maintenance and occasional cable work (T. pp. 11-12). She is right-handed and was working in a 
full duty capacity had no issues with her right hand or right shoulder while employed by 
Respondent before her injury of September 7, 2024 and (T. pp. 12-13). 
 
Petitioner  described  the CTA rodeo event as an annual competition between different departments 
where employees compete in their respective specialties (p. 13). She had not previously 
participated in a competition nor was she involved in setting up the event.  (T. pp. 13-14). Petitioner  
became involved the event when she was asked to be a judge for the signal department competition 
by Mr. Chris Otero, the senior manager of the signal department, about four to five months before 
the rodeo (T. pp. 14-15). She did not work in the signal department (T. p. 14). 
 
Petitioner  said that she was instructed by Senior Manager  Otero  to report to Skokie shop at 6:00 
a.m. on September 7, 2024. She did not work out of the Skokie shop, she was based out of the west 
26IWCC0130

Page 4 of 16 
 
shop.  She was required to wear full personal protective equipment including fire-resistant 
clothing,  FR  jeans, FR shirt,  hard hat, vest, boots, and safety glasses (T. pp. 16-17). Mr. Otero 
instructed her to wear the personal protective requirement  (T. p. 17). If she had not been instructed 
to be a judge, she "probably" would not have attended the event (T. pp. 17-18). 
 
After completing her judging duties for the signal department competition, Petitioner  walked over 
to observe the track department competition where a crowd had gathered (T. p. 18). She testified: 
"I walked toward where they were having the track competition and slid inside of a -- it was like 
a ditch, slid onto the -- in the rocks and tried to brace myself for the slide, for the fall, and -- but 
hit the ground" (T. p. 19).  She fell in the hole. (T. pp. 18-19).  She immediately noticed scraping 
on the outside of her hand, pain going up her arm, and swelling (T. pp. 19). 
 
Petitioner  notified several people immediately, including Mr. Otero who was nearby,  Mr. Mike 
Martello from the signal department, and Mr. Elric Erving, a senior manager who was driving past 
with his son (T. p. 19). Multiple individuals attempted to find an ice pack. Mr. Otero eventually 
improvising by putting ice in a vest bag. After about 30 minutes, she received an ice pack (T. pp. 
19-20). Before she left, a cone was placed in the hole where she fell (T. pp. 20-21). 
 
Petitioner  was sent to Respondent’s occupational health clinic, Concentra, where X-rays were 
taken and she was discharged in a brace and given light duty a restriction of no lifting greater than 
10 pounds with right arm. She followed up with her primary care doctor, Dr Kalal, on September 
9, 2024 who referred her to an orthopedic physician and recommended physical therapy at 
Athletico  (T. pp. 21-22). Dr. Chirag Shah put her hand in a splint on September 17th   and restricted 
her from using her right arm or lifting more than 10 pounds (T. p. 22). X-rays taken on October 1, 
2024 revealed a fracture of the fifth metacarpal (T. p. 23). 
 
On October 15, 2024, when Petitioner  complained of increased shoulder pain during physical 
therapy, Dr. Kalal ordered an MRI and referred her to Dr. Yamaguchi at Northwestern (T. p. 24). 
On November 4, 2024, Dr. Yamaguchi suspected labral tear on November 4, 2024 and performed 
an injection (T. pp. 24-25). She was subsequently referred to Dr. Mara, who confirmed the labral 
tear diagnosis and performed another injection on December 17, 2024 (T .p. 25). Dr. Mara 
recommended surgery. Petitioner  underwent labral repair at Northwestern on February 17, 2025 
(T. pp. 26-27). She completed physical therapy at Athletico and was released to  return to work 
starting  July 7, 2025 (T. pp. 26-27). 
 
Currently, Petitioner experiences sporadic pain, especially with weather changes, morning 
stiffness, and reduced strength, particularly noting: "the reduced strength is what I notice the most" 
(T. p. 28). 
 
Petitioner testified that but for Mr.  Otero asking Petitioner  to judge the signal competition, she 
would not have been in Skokie on the date of the accident. She did not participate in setting  up 
the competition. (T. pp. 28-29).  
 
Under cross-examination, Petitioner  testified that she fell after judging the signal competition.  
She was not done for the day.  She was “instructed to basically stay close by” (T. p. 30).  She was 
not being paid for judging  (T. pp. 31-32).    The rodeo was open to the general public and to CTA 
26IWCC0130

Page 5 of 16 
 
employees and their families. (T. p. 32). When pressed about whether she was "volunteering," she 
consistently responded that she was "asked to be a judge" and participated as a judge because she 
was asked to do so.  Refusing to characterize it as volunteering she answered: “I was asked by a 
senior manager to be a judge and that is why I was there” (T. pp. 31-33).  
 
Petitioner did not sign up for the event through any forms like Survey Monkey nor did she 
complete any other online forms to be a volunteer. She attended the event because she was asked 
by a senior manager, Mr. Otero,  to be a judge (T. pp. 33-34) ). Petitioner served as judge for a 
signal competition designed by Mr. Otero. As a judge, she revealed tools of the trade and materials 
by pulling back a curtain, then gave the competitors three minutes to identify and name as many 
items as possible. After scoring the results, she submitted them to Mr. Otero, who combined her 
event scores with results from other competition sections (T. pp. 34-35). 
 
Petitioner was not assigned any of her regular lineman duties at this jamboree. Her regular work 
schedule at the time was Sunday through Thursday, 3:00 p.m. to 11:30 p.m.; she was not normally 
scheduled to work on Saturdays, the day of the event. Most of the Respondent’s employees that 
attended the event in  did not work that day. (T. pp. 35-36). 
 
Petitioner previously attended the event as a guest but not as an employee (T. pp. 36-37).   When 
asked on cross examination if she felt that was forced to be at the rodeo, she responded: “ That's a 
strong word, forced. No.” (T. p. 38).   
 
On redirect, when asked if she was forced to be there, she responded that she attended because a 
supervisor had asked her to. Just like she did not feel forced to work as an electrician for 
Respondent and agreed she had the right to walk off the job if she wanted to quit (T. pp. 38-39). 
Petitioner testified  that the general public has access to most of her work sites. Petitioner agreed 
that having the public at rodeo is the same as working around the public all the time (T. pp. 39-
40). Petitioner agreed  that the public was not given work boots when they attended the jamboree. 
The public was not required to wear fire resistant clothing when they went to the jamboree. The 
public was not required to wear safety vests when they were at the jamboree. The public was not 
required to wear hard hats when they were at the jamboree. The public was not required to wear 
safety goggles when they went to the jamboree (T. pp. 40-41). 
 
Petitioner contradicted Mr. Erving's earlier testimony, stating she never came to him asking to 
volunteer, never filled out forms, never signed up online, and had no conversations with Mr. Erving 
about volunteering (T. pp. 135-137). She testified that Mr. Otero called her on her cell phone on 
her day off (T. p. 136). She did not work for Mr. Erving (T. 137). When asked if she felt she was 
volunteering, she answered "No. To be in full PPE, arrive at 6:00 a.m., no" (T. p. 137). She stated 
she "would have rather been at home" and that Mr. Otero never told her she would be volunteering 
(T. pp. 138-139). 
 
B. Testimony of Jeannine Messina (CTA Senior Manager) 
Ms. Jeannine Messina is Respondent’s Senior Manager of Infrastructure Administration, 
overseeing 1,165 employees and handling all payroll issues, administrative matters, discipline, 
grievances, arbitrations, and contract negotiations for both exempt and union employees.  She also 
is the  liaison between infrastructure and human resources for hiring, recommendations for 
26IWCC0130

Page 6 of 16 
 
discharge, drug testing, and a plethora of other duties as assigned (T. pp. 42-43). Ms. Messina , 
along with two chairs that run the event, has facilitated the CTA jamboree for 13-15 years , started 
preparation in January for the September event. She attended monthly meetings and biweekly 
meetings as it got close to the event. She helped put everything together for the event throughout 
the year until  the event in September. (T. pp. 44-45). The jamboree has been held for roughly 33 
years (excluding COVID years) and features 9-10 competitions showcasing CTA tradesmen (T. p. 
43). The jamboree is open to all CTA employees and their family and friends. The general public 
also invited (T. p. 45). The various competitions include bus operations, rail operations, 
maintenance, cleanliness, and three infrastructure divisions: track maintenance, power 
maintenance, and signal maintenance (T. pp. 46-47). 
 
Ms. Messina described the volunteer recruitment process, which includes posting flyers, 
distributing applications, and using Survey Monkey for sign-ups. Department heads distribute 
applications to employees (T. pp. 47- 49). She testified she was not aware of any pressure to 
participate or repercussions for not volunteering  (T. pp. 55-56).  Volunteers are not paid nor are 
they required to work if not scheduled for that day (T. p. 56). The event concludes with a banquet 
approximately one month after the jamboree where finalists receive trophy awards. First place 
winners receive three vacation days, gift cards, and additional gifts (pp. 50-51). 
 
Ms. Messina was notified of Petitioner 's injury but not in detail (T. pp. 56-57). It was her 
understanding was that Petitioner  volunteered for the signal maintenance competition but did not 
know in what capacity (T. pp. 57).  She was not notified of any CTA employees who did not want 
to be at the jamboree (T. p. 60).  An employee is not required to wear their uniform while they're 
volunteering (T. p. 64). 
 
Under cross-examination, Ms. Messina testified  that as a salary employee she worked Monday-
Friday 7:00 a.m. through 3:30 p.m.(T. pp. 65-66). The monthly event planning meetings are part 
of her paid job duties (T. p. 71). The event is run by CTA employees Donald Bonds (chief of transit 
operation) and William Mooney (chief infrastructure officer), with Ms. Messina facilitating what 
is  needed.  She noted that there were 5 to 7 people on each committee that help run the event  (T. 
pp. 66-69).  The banquet, the food, the awards was all paid by Respondent (T. p.71).  
 
Ms. Messina testified that the rodeo is an all-volunteer event (T. p. 74).  Ms. Messina admitted that 
if someone is told by senior management to be a judge and they are not volunteering, then "yes" it 
would not be voluntary (T. p. 74). Ms. Messina did not investigate the facts and circumstances 
surrounding  the accident. but was aware that the Injury On Duty (IOD) process was followed. (T. 
pp. 75).  She could not recall if shirts were provided at the event but they did so in the past. (T. p. 
78). There were sign-in sheets at the volunteer table to for attendance purpose but she could not 
recall if there was one volunteer table or a volunteer table for each event (T. p. 79).  She also 
testified that she could not  recall any paperwork or documents listing Petitioner  as a volunteer 
(T. pp. 79-80).   
 
C. Testimony of  Elric Erving (CTA General Manager) 
Mr. Elric Erving is the General Manager over Power and Signal Maintenance at CTA, with 11 
years at the agency and 8 years on the maintenance side (T. pp. 81, 84). His responsibilities include 
26IWCC0130

Page 7 of 16 
 
overseeing power and signal maintenance crews, approving jobs, maintaining budgets, executing 
training, and administering disciplinary actions (T. p. 82). 
 
He could not  recall what the competitions were at the last jamboree “per se” (T. p. 83).  Mr. Erving 
described attending his third or fourth jamboree, noting he did not  attend some years due to low 
attendance “we just didn't have people there” (T. p. 84). He testified that volunteers, family and 
friends are invited to come (T. p. 85).  His role involved ensuring his groups had their stations 
properly set up and riding around on a gator to ensure competitions ran smoothly (T. pp. 85-86). 
 
Mr. Erving testified that volunteers could sign up by email in response to an email from Ms.  
Jeannine Messina, by a handwritten response “via the application” (T. p. 87), through Survey 
Monkey, or by coming to their respective manager’s  office with an oral response  (T. p. 87). Based 
on his experience as a manager at the CTA, there no  pressure from management on employees of 
CTA to participate in the events at the jamboree nor was there any repercussions for an employee 
that declines to attend whether as a competitor or as a volunteer (T. pp. 89-90).  
 
Mr. Erving testified that Petitioner  was "volunteering for the signal maintenance competition to 
help set up, oversee the signal maintenance competition" (T. p. 91) and was "in charge of 
overseeing the competitions, whether it was timing, scoring, general setup, general takedown" (T. 
p. 103) ). Although he did not recall when , Mr. Erving claimed he recalled having a conversation 
with  Petitioner  about her wanting to volunteer and   having  received both verbal confirmation 
and a physical application and a form that would include her T-shirt size (T. pp. 104-105). 
 
Under cross-examination, Mr. Erving confirmed he was Petitioner 's supervisor for about two 
years. He characterized her as trustworthy, honest, safe, and  a hard worker (T. p. 101). Mr. Erving 
testified that there should be a list of volunteers so they could get T-shirt sizes so everyone running 
the event would know who the volunteers are (T. p. 102). He claimed to have Petitioner  on his 
volunteer list via email but did not bring it to the hearing (T. p. 102). He noted that Petitioner could 
not have volunteered to judge a lineman competition because there was no competition that day 
for lineman (T. p. 111).  
 
Mr. Erving was instructed his bosses to fill out the supervisor's report of employee injury on duty 
because the accident being on CTA property (T. pp. 111-112), noting unsafe conditions as "defect" 
and "slick surface" (T. p. 116), and recommending that the "sink hole should be fixed in the ballast 
track area to prevent further slips and falls"(T. p. 114). He described the sink hole as something 
you "can't visually see...until you step in one" (T. pp. 117). 
 
The report indicated Petitioner  started work at 6:00 a.m., with all volunteers and competitors 
arriving before the 8:00 a.m. public opening (T. p. 119). Mr.  Erving noted that while he was not  
Petitioner 's day-to-day supervisor, "her being the volunteer for my groups that day I was her 
supervisor" (T. p. 120). 
 
The record shows that Nick Schiro, listed as Petitioner 's manager, authorized treatment at 
Concentra for a work-related injury (T. pp. 129-130). Where as in his own IOD report, Mr. Erving 
wrote  that the employee was "volunteering," including in the job description field where he wrote 
"Line worker (volunteering)" and in the incident description: "employee who was volunteering for 
26IWCC0130

Page 8 of 16 
 
2024 rodeo" (T. pp. 132). When asked about this, he confirmed it was his understanding of her 
status on September 7, 2024; that she was “interested” (T. p. 133). 
 
D. Medical Evidence 
On September 7, 2024, Petitioner presented to Concentra River West. She was diagnosed with a 
right shoulder strain, contusion of hand and contusion of right elbow and forearm and  given work

III, CONCLUSIONS OF LAW 
 
The Arbitrator adopts the above Findings of Fact in support of the Conclusions of Law set forth 
below. Section 1(d) of the Act provides that, to obtain compensation under the Act, Petitioner bears 
the burden of showing, by a preponderance of the evidence, that he or she has sustained accidental 
injuries arising out of and in the course of the employment. 820 ILCS 305/1(d). To obtain 
compensation under the Act, Petitioner has the burden of proving, by a preponderance of the 
evidence, all of the elements of his or her claim. O’Dette v. Industrial Commission, 79 Ill. 2d 249, 
253 (1980) including that there is some causal relationship between the employment and the injury 
Caterpillar Tractor Co. v. Industrial Commission, 129 Ill. 2d 52, 63 (1989). And yet, it also is well 
established that the Act is humane law of remedial nature and is to be liberally construed to affect 
the purpose of the Act that the burdens of caring for the casualties of industry should be borne by 
the industry and not by the individuals who misfortunes arise out of the industry, nor by public. 
Shell Oil v Industrial Commission, 2 III 2nd 590, 603 (1954).  The Act should be liberally construed 
to provide financial protection for injured workers. McAllister v Illinois Workers’ Compensation 
Commission.  2020 IL 124848. The Act’s provisions are to be read in harmony to achieve that 
goal. Vaught v Industrial Commission, 52 Ill. 2d 158,165 (1972). Injured workers are entitled to 
“prompt, sure and definite compensation, together with a quick and efficient remedy” with industry 
bearing the “costs of such industries: rather than the injured worker. O’Brien v Rautenbush, 10 
III.2d 167, 174 (1956). Decisions of an arbitrator shall be based exclusively on stipulation of the 
parties, the evidence in the record of proceeding and material that has been officially noticed.  
 
Credibility finding of Petitioner: The Arbitrator, as the trier of fact in this case, has the 
responsibility to observe the witnesses testify, judge their credibility, and determine how much 
weight to afford their testimony and the other evidence presented. The Arbitrator observed 
Petitioner during the hearing and finds her to be a credible witness. The Arbitrator compared 
Petitioner’s testimony with the totality of the evidence submitted and did not find any material 
contradictions that would deem the witness unreliable.  
WITH RESPECT TO ISSUE (C), DID AN ACCIDENT OCCUR THAT AROSE OUT OF 
AND IN THE COURSE OF PETITIONER'S EMPLOYMENT BY RESPONDENT THE 
ARBITRATOR FINDS AS FOLLOWS: 
 
The pivotal issue presented in this claim  is whether Respondent is liable for Petitioner’s accidental 
injuries which she sustained while participating in Respondent’s recreational event as a judge -  
did she do so voluntarily or was she ordered or assigned to participate.  The governing statutory 
provision addressing this issue is Section 11 of the Act  which provides in relevant part: 
“Accidental injuries incurred while participating in voluntary recreational programs including but 
not limited to athletic events, parties and picnics do not arise out of and in the course of the 
employment even though the employer pays some or all of the cost thereof. This exclusion shall 
not apply in the event that the injured employee was ordered or assigned by his employer to 
participate in the program.” [Emphasis added] 
 
Accordingly, an employer is responsible for accidental injuries sustained at a recreational 
programs such as the CTA Rodeo Jamboree when the employee is ordered or assigned by her 
26IWCC0130

Page 10 of 16 
 
employer to participate.  There is no dispute that Respondent sponsored the rodeo. The is no 
dispute that it was intended to be a recreational event. Respondent organized, paid for, and ran the 
jamboree.  Ms. Messina testified she spent over 8 months planning the event.  It is further 
undisputed that the rodeo was a promotional activity which inured to the benefit of Respondent.  It 
also cannot be disputed that Respondent benefited from Petitioner’s participation as a judge of the 
competition. However, the question of employer control and benefit has no bearing upon whether 
the activity was recreational in nature. The determining  issue has been and is whether Petitioner’s 
participation was voluntary. Cary Fire Protection District v. Industrial Comm'n ,  211 Ill. App. 3d 
20 (1991).  The Arbitrator notes that the extent to which Respondent benefits from 
Petitioner’s participation, the extent to which Respondent  actively organizes and runs the 
recreational event, and the extent to which Respondent sponsors and encourages 
attendance in the event are still legitimate inquiries.  They are only important insofar as to whether 
the activity is voluntary. They have no bearing whatsoever on whether the activity is a 
recreational program as defined by the Act. 
  
In Fischer v. Industrial Comm’n, 142 Ill. App. 3d 298, 303 (1986), the appellate court  reviewed 
cases involving recreational activities and the criteria for determining whether the recreational 
activity itself arises out of and in the course of employment. The Fischer court stated that  the 
individual facts of each recreational activity must be carefully reviewed along the following 
principal lines of inquiry: (1) to what extent the employer benefits from the employee's attendance 
at the outing; (2) to what extent the employer actively organizes and runs the recreational 
attendance at the event; and (3) to what extent the employer sponsors and compels attendance at 
the event. The evidence in this case must be analyzed under the three foregoing lines of inquiry. 
 
The Commission and the Appellate Court has found compensable injuries sustained while 
participating in various recreational activities, including, while playing basketball, CTA v. 
Industrial Commission, 238 Ill.App.3rd 224 (1987),  while playing soccer, Parks v. Chicago 
Community Loan Fund, 23 IWCC 0183; while giving a speech at a retirement party, Pinckneyville 
Community Hospital v. Industrial Commission, 365 Ill.App.3d 1062, and while playing volleyball, 
Lay v. Tri-C Elementary, 20 IWCC 0337. In Parks, the Commission found injuries sustained in a 
company soccer match were compensable under the Act, as Petitioner credibly testified her belief 
that participation in the soccer match was mandatory, despite Respondent’s assertion that it was 
voluntary.  23 IWCC 0183. As in Parks, Petitioner believed that her participation was mandatory. 
 
Consistent with Petitioner’s testimony that she believed that she was injured on duty is 
Respondent’s ‘ Employee’s Report of Injury on Duty” form completed by Petitioner on September 
9, 2024 wherein she reported injuring her right hand, right arm and right shoulder when she slid in 
a ditch on CTA property and fell backward with her right arm extended and landed on her right 
arm and shoulder. Notably, she did not  mention being a volunteer. (Pet. Ex. 6, p. 4).   
 
On the other hand, Mr. Erving completed Respondent’s “Supervisor’s Report of Employee Injured 
on Duty” form indicating that Petitioner was a “volunteer” (Pet. Ex. 6, pp. 5-6). His report is 
consistent with his testimony.   
 
In weighing the credible evidence, the Arbitrator concludes that Petitioner was required to attend 
by a CTA supervisor rather than participating on a voluntary basis. This determination is supported 
26IWCC0130

Page 11 of 16 
 
by the following findings: First, Petitioner provided testimony that she was obligated to wear 
protective clothing and personal protective equipment, which distinguished her from other 
attendees. Notably, Respondent's witnesses did not indicate that she was wearing a volunteer T-
shirt that would have been consistent with volunteer status. 
 
Second,  Petitioner was instructed to arrive at 6 a.m., two hours before attendees were allowed in 
the event. One can easily believe  Petitioner testimony  that she did not want to appear to the rodeo 
so early in the morning when her  normal workday started at 3:00 p.m..   Given this and the 
commuting from her home time to the event, it is not difficult to accept that Petitioner was not 
inclined to volunteer for an unpaid event so early in the morning, on her day off  and so outside 
her normal circadian schedule.  It is  more likely to believe that she was assigned  to be a judge 
and that is was reasonable for her to believe that her attendance was mandatory. Her pre-accident 
and post-accident conduct was consistent with her belief.  Moreover, Petitioner attended the event 
without any family or friends, which is not necessarily consistent with volunteer status, as other 
volunteers, like Mr. Erving were encouraged to and did bring family and friends. 
 
Third, the Arbitrator notes that Respondent did not offer testimony from Mr. Otero to refute 
Petitioner’s testimony that he directed her to serve as a judge of the competition.  He was the 
witness who was in the best position to confirm or dispute Petitioner’s testimony, one way or 
another. He did not.  
 
Fourth, Respondent failed to submit any lists identifying Petitioner as a volunteer at the event, 
despite Mr. Erving’s testimony that he had an email of the volunteer list.  Respondent failed to 
submit the  written application which should have been completed for Petitioner to serve as a 
volunteer, a requirement described by both Ms. Messina and Mr. Erving.  In fact, Respondent 
failed to submit any contemporaneous documents prior to her accident to support its claim that 
Petitioner was a volunteer.   
 
Fifth,  Ms. Messina testified that although the rodeo is an all-volunteer event she admitted on cross 
examination  that if an employee is told by senior management to be a judge,  they are not 
volunteering, then "yes" it would not be voluntary (T. p. 74). 
 
It is well settled under  the law that where a party fails to produce evidence in his control, the 
presumption arises that the evidence would be adverse to that party.  Saunders v. Department of 
Public Aid 198 Ill. App.3d 1076, 1082. (1990),  Reo Movers v. Industrial Commission, 226 
Ill.App.3d 216 (1992). In Singh v. Air Illinois, Inc.,  165 Ill. App.3d 923 (1988) , the court held 
that a jury should not be instructed on such a presumption where the evidence showed that there 
was a reasonable excuse for the failure to produce the evidence and that the evidence was equally 
available to the other side. However, in In re Marriage of Leff (1986), 148 Ill. App.3d 792, the 
court allowed the presumption where the wife failed to present any evidence as to the value of her 
husband's business even though she had clearly attempted to gather such evidence.   
 
In the present matter, Respondent offered no excuse for its failure to provide  written evidence that 
would have corroborated its assertion that Petitioner served as a volunteer. Furthermore, 
Respondent presented no explanation for failing to call Mr. Otero as a witness even though he was 
still employed by Respondent.

Page 12 of 16 
 
 
In summary, the Arbitrator is mindful of  the  inconsistencies in the evidence. Most notably, there 
is a direct conflict between Mr. Erving's assertion that Petitioner initiated contact with him to 
volunteer although his recollection of the circumstances were foggy. In contrast, Petitioner's 
contradictory testimony denying this ever occurred was straight forward, consistent and 
unequivocal. Petitioner explicitly stated that she had not approached Mr. Erving, she had not 
completed any forms, she had not registered online, and she had not discussed volunteering with 
Mr. Erving (T. pp. 135-136). Furthermore, the Arbitrator finds that Petitioner’s testimony is 
consistent with the evidence as a whole, while Mr. Erving's testimony is not. 
  
Despite claims of formal written volunteer processes, no documentation was produced showing 
Petitioner  as a volunteer. Ms. Messina could not recall any paperwork listing Petitioner  as a 
volunteer and while Mr. Erving claimed to have an email list of volunteers, he did not  bring it to 
the hearing, nor a copy of the application, nor  the volunteer participant sign in sheet for the day 
of the event.    
 
Petitioner  consistently testified that Mr. Otero, the senior manager of the signal department, called 
her on her cell phone on her day off, 4-5 months before the event, asking her to judge the signal 
competition. This contradicts the narrative of voluntary sign-up processes described by Ms. 
Messina and Mr. Erving. 
 
The evidence indicates that despite Respondent’s  significant efforts to have a successful and well 
attended rodeo, it did not have as many volunteers as it would have liked. Respondent has had 
issues with low attendance in the past. And  Petitioner’s department did not enter the competition 
at the September 7, 2024 rodeo, possibly due to a lack of volunteers.  Mr. Otero needed volunteers 
for his department and apparently recruited. The facts and circumstances surrounding this issue 
reminds this Arbitrator of the military concept of being "voluntold" - where an individual is 
ostensibly volunteering but is actually following orders from a superior. This situation mirrors the 
classic combat scenario where a commanding officer declares, "I need three volunteers - you, you, 
and you."  The evidence is consistent with Petitioner being “voluntold” by Mr. Otero.  
 
The requirement for full PPE including fire-resistant clothing, hard hat, vest, boots, and safety 
glasses distinguishes Petitioner 's role from typical volunteers, who according to testimony 
received T-shirts and were told to wear the volunteer shirts for  the benefit of the attendees. The 
form allegedly completed by Petitioner indicating her volunteer shirt size was not produced. 
 
The fact that Respondent processed her injury as an injury on duty (IOD), with Mr. Erving filling 
out supervisor reports as instructed by his bosses and Mr. Schiro authorizing medical treatment for 
a work-related injury, suggests Respondent initially treated this as work-related activity rather than 
voluntary participation. The Arbitrator does not, however, find that the IOD process constitutes as 
an admission against interest. 
 
The Arbitrator finds that Petitioner's recollection of events concerning the threshold issue was 
clearer and more consistent than that of Ms. Messina and Mr. Erving. Ms. Messina and Mr. Erving 
occasionally contradicted one another. For instance, Mr. Erving testified that volunteers were 
required to wear shirts identifying them as such, while Ms. Messina believed the shirts were

Page 13 of 16 
 
unavailable that year and not mandatory. Neither witness noted that she was wearing a shirt 
designating Petitioner as a volunteer.  
 
The Arbitrator finds that Ms. Messina and Mr. Erving recollection of the events surrounding the 
critical issue in this case was not as consistent as that of Petitioner.  Respondent’s witnesses 
testified as what they believed should have occurred, not necessarily what in fact occurred in regard 
to Petitioner’s volunteer status or assigned status.  Whereas Petitioner’s testimony was consistent,  
consistent with the evidence and consistent with common sense.  The Arbitrator therefore finds  
Petitioner’s testimony to be more reliable and persuasive than the sincere but fuzzy recollected 
testimony of Ms. Messina and Mr. Erving.  
 
The Arbitrator finds that Petitioner has proven by a preponderance of the  evidence that she  
sustained her injury while participating as a judge in the rodeo as directed by Supervisor Chris 
Otero. Accordingly, the evidence has demonstrated the Petitioner sustained an injury that arose 
out of and in the course of her employment and was not barred by Section 11 of the Act.  
 
WITH RESPECT TO ISSUE (F), IS PETITIONER’S CURRENT CONDITION OF ILL-
BEING CAUSALLY RELATED TO THE INJURY, THE ARBITRATOR FINDS AS 
FOLLOWS:  
 
In a workers' compensation case, the claimant has the burden of proving, by a preponderance of the 
evidence, all of the elements of his claim." R & D Thiel v. Illinois Workers' Compensation Comm'n, 
398 Ill. App. 3d 858, 867 (2010). A preexisting condition does not prevent recovery under the Act 
if that condition was aggravated or accelerated by the claimant's employment. Absolute 
Cleaning/SVMBL v. Illinois Workers' Compensation Comm'n, 409 Ill. App. 3d 463, 470 (2011), 
quoting Caterpillar Tractor Co. v. Industrial Comm'n, 92 Ill. 2d 30, 36 (1982).  Further, every 
natural consequence that flows from an injury that arose out of and in the course of the claimant's 
employment is compensable unless caused by an independent intervening accident that breaks the 
chain of causation between a work-related injury and an ensuing disability or injury. Vogel v. Illinois 
Workers' Compensation. Comm'n, 354 Ill. App. 3d 780 (2005). "That other incident, whether work-
related or not, may have aggravated the claimant's condition is irrelevant." Vogel, 354 Ill. App. 3d 
at 786. To obtain compensation under the Act, a claimant must prove that some act or phase of his 
employment was a causative factor in his ensuing injuries.  A work-related injury need not be the 
sole or principal causative factor, as long as it was a causative factor in the resulting condition of 
ill-being.  Sisbro, Inc. v. Industrial Comm'n, 207 Ill. 2d 193 (2003). 
 
It has long been held that “a chain of events which demonstrates a previous condition of good 
health, an accident, and a subsequent injury resulting in disability may be sufficient circumstantial 
evidence to prove a causal nexus between the accident and the employee’s injury.”  Int’l Harvester 
v. Indus. Comm’n, 93 Ill. 2d 59, 63-64 (1982).  When the claimant’s version of the accident is 
uncontradicted and his testimony is unimpeached, his recital of the facts surrounding the accident 
may be sufficient to sustain an award.  Id. at 64.  An employer takes its employees as it finds them. 
St. Elizabeth Hospital v Worker’s Compensation Comm’n, 371 Ill. App 3d 882, 888 (2007).  That 
Petitioner had a pre-existing condition does not preclude the use of a chain of events analysis. 
Schroeder v Illinois Worker’s Compensation Commission, 2017 Ill. App.(4th) 160192 WC (2017); 
26IWCC0130

Page 14 of 16 
 
Corn Belt Energy Corp. v Illinois Worker’s Compensation Commission, 2016 Ill. App (3d) 150311 
WC.   
 
In the present case, the evidence revealed that Petitioner had a preexisting asymptomatic  condition  
to her right shoulder and wrist. Petitioner disclosed in the Employee’s Report of Injury on Duty 
that she had arthroscopic surgery of her right wrist  and rotator cuff and acromion surgery in 2011 
(Pet Ex 6, p. 4). Her volunteered information was corroborated by the medical evidence. On 
September 7, 2024,  Petitioner  injured her right upper extremity  that led to ongoing uninterrupted 
pain in the right shoulder. When conservative treatments failed to alleviate her shoulder pain, pain 
corroborated  by objective findings, surgery was recommended by Dr. Marra at Northwestern.  
 
The mechanism of injury where she slipped and fell with an outstretched arm to brace her fall 
aligns with the Petitioner’s injury and symptoms, and Petitioner was disabled after her fall. There 
is  no evidence presented of intervening or subsequent injuries to her  that could explain 
Petitioner’s injuries and current condition. The evidence and the medical histories in the record 
demonstrate a consistent history as to the onset of Petitioner’s shoulder work injury being on 
September 7, 2024, histories that correlate with Petitioner’s testimony.  Therefore, there is no 
evidence that would lead the Arbitrator to determine that the Petitioner’s current condition of her 
right shoulder was caused by anything other than the September 7, 2024 injury.  
 
The Arbitrator has carefully reviewed and considered all the medical and documentary evidence, 
along with the all the testimony and finds that Petitioner has proven by a preponderance of the 
evidence that her accidental injury caused her condition of ill-being related right shoulder and 
upper extremity  such that her current condition of ill-being can be said to have been causally-
connected to work injury due to the chain of events and not simply the result of a normal 
degenerative process of the pre-existing condition. 
 
Pursuant to the Sisbro case, it is clear that a work-related accident that aggravates or accelerates a 
pre-existing condition can be compensable. Based on the documentary evidence, Petitioner had a 
preexisting right shoulder condition and wrist condition. However, the chain of events presented 
in this case show her right shoulder  problem made worse by her  accident.  For the 5  years prior 
to her September 7,2024 accident, Petitioner was never taken off work due to shoulder pain 
although she had a physical job as a lineman. During this period of time, Petitioner performed her 
job duties on a daily basis.  The Arbitrator notes that Respondent witnessed  voiced no  complaints 
about Petitioner’s pre-accident work performance.  In fact, Mr. Erving testified that she was an 
honest and hard worker. No mention was made that Petitioner missed time off work because of 
her preexisting right upper extremity issues no mention was made that she requested any 
accommodation because of a preexisting shoulder condition. It is undisputed that Petitioner’s 
position was physical.  
 
The Arbitrator finds that the record shows that accident caused Petitioner’s shoulder pathology, 
the need for  treatment and the need for  surgery. There is  no  evidence  of intervening or 
subsequent injuries   that could explain Petitioner’s injuries and current condition. The medical 
histories in the record demonstrate a consistent history as to the onset of Petitioner’s shoulder work 
injury being on September 7, 2024,  histories that correlate with Petitioner’s testimony.  The 
Arbitrator finds,  based on the weight of the credible evidence in the record, that Petitioner’s 
26IWCC0130

Page 15 of 16 
 
current condition of ill-being is causally related to the work accident based on the chain of events 
and  the medical evidence submitted into the record. Accordingly, the Arbitrator finds that 
Petitioner has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that her  right shoulder labral tear and 
fracture of the right fifth metacarpal are causally connected to her work accident of September 7, 
2024.  The Arbitrator also  finds that the September 7, 2024 accident caused the need for the 
surgery performed by Dr. Marra to the right shoulder.

WITH RESPECT TO ISSUE (L), WHAT AMOUNT OF COMPENSATION IS DUE FOR  
TEMPORARY TOTAL DISABILITY, TEMPORARY PARTIAL DISABILITY AND/OR  
MAINTENANCE, THE ARBITRATOR FINDS AS FOLLOWS: 
 
A claimant is temporarily totally disabled from the time an injury incapacitates him from work 
until such time as he is as far recovered or restored as the permanent character of his injury will 
permit. Westin Hotel v. Indus. Comm'n, 372 Ill.App.3d 527, 542 (1st Dist. 2007). In determining 
whether a claimant remains entitled to receiving temporary total disability benefits, the primary 
consideration is whether the claimant's condition has stabilized and whether he is capable of a 
return to the workforce. Interstate Scaffolding, Inc. v. Illinois Workers' Comp. Comm'n, 236 Ill.2d 
132, 148 (2010). Once an injured employee's physical condition stabilizes, he is no longer eligible 
for temporary total disability benefits. Archer Daniels Midland Co. v. Indus. Comm'n, 138 Ill.2d 
107, 118 (1990). 
 
The medical documentation and Petitioner’s testimony demonstrate that her treating physicians 
either took her  off work or imposed work restrictions that Respondent did  not accommodate. 
from September 8, 2024 through July 1, 2025, the last medical office visit. Petitioner testified her 
delayed returned to work on July 7, 2025 was due to Respondent’s return to work procedures.   
Based on the above findings, the Arbitrator finds that Respondent is responsible for temporary 
total disability benefits in the amount of $1,642.83/week for a period of 43 -1/7 weeks for the 
period of September 8, 2024 through July 6, 2025, the period that she was unable to work but for 
her work injury.

WITH RESPECT TO ISSUE (M), SHOULD PENALTIES BE IMPOSED UPON THE  
RESPONDENT, THE ARBITRATOR FINDS AS FOLLOWS: 
 
A trial  is designed to search for the truth. After considering all the facts and circumstances in the 
record, the Arbitrator concludes that imposing penalties or fees is not justified. The Arbitrator 
acknowledges his concern  about inconsistencies in the  testimony of Respondent’s witnesses in 
relation to the presented evidence. The Arbitrator  is also troubled by Respondent’s failure to 
produce supporting documentation  which would have corroborated Petitioner being a volunteer 
and fails to understand why Respondent the failed to call Mr. Ortero. The Arbitrator does not 
believe it was to the lack of diligence by its trial attorney. Respondent is well represented by a 
skilled, competent  and professional attorney who zealously represents his client.  
 
On the other hand, Ms. Messina and Mr. Erving appeared to be sincere in their belief that Petitioner 
was a volunteer.  And understandably so.  The event was intended to be a volunteer recreational  
event.  However, the evidence suggests that there may not have been enough of the willing, there 
may not have been enough of those willing to be volunteers. In this case, the evidence supports 
the finding that  Petitioner was not willing a volunteer; rather she was voluntold by Mr. Otero.  She 
was assigned to be a judge.   
 
Although the inconsistencies in Respondent’s defense cast doubt on the viability of the defense, 
the Arbitrator finds that Respondent approached the edge of the Rubicon, and may have even 
waded in it,   but Respondent did not cross it. Benefits were not paid under the Act. Benefits were 
denied because Respondent relied upon Section 11 of the Act as the event was intended to be a 
recreational event. Respondent chose to have the dispute resolved by trial and took no actions to 
delay the trial. After considering all the facts and circumstances of the case, the Arbitrator 
concludes that the imposition of penalties or fees is not justified. Respondent's actions were neither 
unreasonable nor vexatious in this instance. Respondent believed it had a legitimate basis for 
disputing the accident under Section 11 of the Act. As a result, Petitioner’s request for penalties 
and attorney fees is denied.
